summary.text: A 42-year-old active-duty man with a five-pack-year smoking history, pulmonary nodules, prior DVT, chronic anemia, alcohol use disorder and a possible prior RA diagnosis (earlier RF-positive, anti-CCP-negative serology, with methotrexate or hydroxychloroquine declined) presented to the emergency department after two to three days of worsening cough, dyspnea and weakness and a three-month, 20-pound weight loss. He was afebrile, tachypneic and tachycardic (130/min) with bilateral crackles, SpO2 85% on 2 L nasal cannula and blood pressure 110s/60s.

Initial labs showed severe macrocytic anemia (Hb 6.8 g/dL), sodium 129 mEq/L, AST 273/ALT 83 U/L and D-dimer 1744 ng/mL with mild proteinuria and negative respiratory viral and bacterial PCR panels. Chest CT angiography excluded pulmonary embolism and showed extensive bilateral consolidation, ground-glass and nodular opacities. He received one unit of red cells and empiric IV cefepime and doxycycline, was admitted to the floor, and was moved to the ICU the next morning for worsening work of breathing, tachypnea and hypoxemia. Family history included dermatomyositis in a first-degree relative.

Bronchoscopic transbronchial biopsies showed uniform interstitial inflammation and fibrosis consistent with NSIP, with BAL negative for bacterial, viral and fungal pathogens; inflammatory markers were elevated. Autoimmune serology was positive for ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-RNP, anti-Sm/RNP, anti-chromatin and RF with negative anti-CCP and low C3, supporting a possible diagnosis of MCTD; rheumatology concurred with management. The abstract states a final diagnosis of MCTD-associated NSIP while the body calls it possible/suspected.

Treatment was IV methylprednisolone 60 mg every eight hours for two days then 500 mg daily for three days, with negative cultures and BAL AFB; respiratory status improved, oxygen was weaned off, and oral prednisone 60 mg daily with taper was started. After appropriate baseline studies MMF was started at 500 mg twice daily and increased to 1,000 mg twice daily. Echocardiography showed sinus tachycardia up to 120 bpm with normal LV function and no valvular, right heart or pulmonary hypertension findings; the tachycardia resolved.

He was discharged with close outpatient pulmonology, rheumatology and gastroenterology follow-up arranged and an outpatient colonoscopy scheduled for chronic anemia. Bilateral lower-extremity paresthesias suggestive of autoimmune neuropathy were treated with gabapentin, and outpatient EMG and neurology follow-up were recommended. Follow-up chest CT showed marked improvement at one month and near-complete resolution at six months.

ambiguities.description: MCTD certainty differs across the article: the abstract says the patient was ultimately diagnosed with MCTD-associated NSIP after confirmatory serologies, whereas the body says the serologies support a possible MCTD diagnosis and the MMF indication is suspected MCTD-associated NSIP. Biopsy-consistent NSIP is kept as a diagnosis; MCTD is kept as possible; the combined confirmed claim is review-only. Do not infer a confirmed MCTD diagnosis.

article_limitations: Figure pixels were inspected separately in the visual submission; the annotation figures[] keep caption-layer status not_inspected by convention.
MCTD diagnostic certainty is internally inconsistent (abstract confirmed vs body possible/suspected); not reconciled.
Potassium 5.0 mEq/L is flagged High although equal to the printed upper reference limit; kept as printed.
Complement C4 is reported as a range (16-27 mg/dL) without a single value; no bounds were split.

Timing relative to other events is explicit for few events (one- and six-month follow-up CT, ICU transfer the following morning, steroid durations); the rest is ordered only where the text words it. Outpatient colonoscopy, EMG and neurology follow-up are planned/recommended, not documented as completed.
The article is a single-patient report; no cited cases or supplements are assigned to the patient. Background statements about NSIP/MCTD are not patient facts.
Possible etiologies for abnormal labs and the tachycardia are authors’ hypotheses and are not recorded as diagnoses.
